newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Bitter rights battle rages for Russian steel mill.
newsitem.headline: Bitter rights battle rages for Russian steel mill.

text.p: Angry foreign investors claiming a majority share in a huge Soviet steel mill have vowed to bring business at the annual meeting to a halt in a battle for representation which could shape Russian shareholder rights.

A group of outside investors who have joined forces against the management of Novolipetsk Metallurgical Plant (NLMK), 400 km (250 miles) south of Moscow, say they will withdraw support on every issue at Saturday's annual meeting.

A lengthy battle for control has focused foreign investor attention on the smelter, which is worth almost $1 billion dollars and produced some seven million tonnes of steel in 1996 and 1995, Itar-Tass news agency said.
"This is definitely a key case for shareholder rights," said spokesman Yuri Kotler of the Federal Commission for the Securities Market.
The securities watchdog is helpless to address the alleged breach of joint stock company law, he added. The commission has no power to enforce that law.

Salomon Bros-advised Cambridge Capital Management, Sputnik Funds and Russia's ICFI (Bank MFK) say they have over 50 percent of steel mill shares, and a local court has backed their claim that the annual meeting must consider their candidates for places on the board.

But management has appealed against the latest ruling. It says that while the matter is still in court the annual meeting can proceed, and outsiders' candidatures to the board need not even be considered.
"This assertion has nothing in common with the real state of affairs," Novolipetsk's board of directors said in a statement on Friday.

Sputnik Fund managing director Gregory Bedrosian said in a statement -- "It appears that NLMK management believes it can operate openly outside the law with invalid, unelected directors and take decisions at an illegal annual general meeting that they have stage managed."

Foreigners' investments have helped drive the leading RTS stock market index up 150 percent this year. They have billions of dollars at stake in Russian industry, now that privatisation and industrial reform are in full swing.
Kotler said outside shareholders throughout Russia were increasingly pressing for representation. "This year and next year will be a struggle for control," he said.
"From the point of view of ownership it is critical, because insiders and outsiders are 50-50 (in Russian industry generally)."

Rutgers University professor Joseph Blasi, who has studied Russia's leading companies, said outsiders owned an average 58 percent of the biggest Russian companies, with the remainder almost evenly split between workers and the state.
"There is a tremendous amount of foreign investment that is subject to issues similar to this," said a Western shares analyst in Moscow.

Foreign investors in multi-billion dollar Russian oil production companies, the largest sector of the stock market, are worried by attempts by oil holding companies to consolidate the separately-traded units, the analyst said.
Some fear holding companies considered overvalued will ride rough-shod over minority holders as they try to acquire production unit shares and consolidate at rock-bottom prices.
Novolipetsk management says some of the company shares in outsiders' hands are non-voting shares, a claim backed by a local court but also under appeal.
So the battle will only become clear at the meeting when each side musters voting blocks.

The outside investors have vowed to call an extraordinary meeting if their board slate is not voted on and are continuing a number of court battles. The fireworks at the weekend meeting are unlikely to end this particular battle.
